title: Top N most-frequent words
instructorPromptText: Write a function that takes a paragraph of text and an integer n, and returns the n most-frequent words as a list. Words are case-insensitive. Break ties alphabetically.

specGateDimensions.description: What counts as a 'word' — whitespace-separated tokens, or alphabetic sequences with punctuation stripped? Does "don't" count as one word or two?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Tokenization is the hidden core of this problem; the student must commit before coding or they will silently conflate 'word.' and 'word' as distinct entries.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the function return if n exceeds the number of distinct words in the paragraph?
specGateDimensions.rationale: This is the canonical boundary case for top-n problems; committing in the spec prevents an IndexError-or-not ambiguity.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the function return when n is 0 or negative?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt assumes n is sensible; forcing a commitment surfaces whether the student will validate, return [], or let it crash.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the function return for an empty string or a string containing only whitespace/punctuation?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Empty input is the most-missed case and interacts with the n-vs-vocab question.

specGateDimensions.description: Is the returned list a list of words only, or a list of (word, count) pairs? In what case are the returned words (original casing or lowercased)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt says 'list of words' but students often return tuples with counts; and case-insensitive counting does not specify case-insensitive output.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the alphabetical tie-break apply only among words with equal frequency, or is the full ordering frequency-then-alphabetical?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Students often sort alphabetically first and then by frequency unstably, or vice versa, producing wrong results on ties.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student's spec commits to stripping punctuation but code uses `text.split()` only, so 'word.' and 'word' are counted as different tokens
Case-insensitivity is stated in spec but code forgets to lowercase before counting, or lowercases for counting but returns the original-case form inconsistently
Alphabetical tie-break is specified but code uses `sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])` without a secondary key, giving dict-insertion-order ties

Plan describes building a dict manually with `if word in counts` branches; code uses `collections.Counter` and `.most_common()` — coherent stdlib substitution (but note: `.most_common()` does not alphabetize ties)
Plan sorts then slices; code uses a heap of size n — coherent optimization, valid if correctness is preserved
Sort key negates frequency for descending order but leaves word ascending, which works, versus sorting twice and losing stability — subtle correctness bug on ties
Uses `sort()` (returns None) where `sorted()` was intended, causing the function to return None
Slices with `[:n]` without handling n > len, which happens to work in Python but the student's spec may have promised an error
